title: There are some wounds that never fully leave a person’s body.
paragraphs: There are some wounds that never fully leave a person’s body.
Not because God abandoned them.
Not because healing was impossible.
But because trauma changes the way someone sees love long before they ever experience it.
Mephibosheth was only five years old when his entire world collapsed.
Five.

The age where children still reach for their father’s hand in crowded places.
The age where safety is supposed to feel permanent.
The age where fear leaves fingerprints on the soul forever.
And in one single afternoon, Mephibosheth lost everything.

His grandfather Saul was dead.
His father Jonathan was dead.
The kingdom was collapsing.
Panic consumed the palace.
And then Scripture quietly records one of the most devastating moments in the entire Bible.

“His nurse took him up, and fled: and it came to pass, as she made haste to flee, that he fell, and became lame.”
— 2 Samuel 4:4
The Hebrew phrase here is painfully vivid.

“וַיִּפֹּל” (vayyippol)
“He fell.”

Not stumbled.
Not injured.
Fell.
The kind of fall that changes a life permanently.

And the Hebrew word for lame is:
“פִּסֵּחַ” (pisseach)

crippled,
halted,
disabled,
unable to walk normally again.

Before Mephibosheth ever understood politics…
before he understood kingship…
before he understood covenant…
he learned trauma.
He learned instability.
He learned loss.
He learned what it felt like to be dropped while everyone else was trying to save themselves.
Some people reading this know exactly what that feels like.
You were not intentionally destroyed…
but you were dropped.

Dropped by parents who were emotionally absent.
Dropped by people who promised forever.
Dropped by churches that preached love but practiced cruelty.
Dropped by friends.
Dropped by leadership.
Dropped by betrayal.
Dropped by abandonment.
Dropped during moments when somebody else’s panic became your lifelong pain.
And what makes trauma even harder is this:
Mephibosheth did absolutely nothing wrong.
Nothing.
He was wounded because of what happened around him.
That is the hidden agony inside this story.
Some people carry consequences from battles they never started.
And trauma has a terrifying way of changing identity.
Years later, David searches for anyone left from the house of Saul because of his covenant with Jonathan.
Not obligation.
Covenant.

The Hebrew word is:
“חֶסֶד” (chesed)
One of the deepest words in Scripture.

It means:
steadfast covenant mercy,
loyal lovingkindness,
undeserved faithful love.
Not temporary kindness.
Covenant love that refuses to disappear.
David asks:

“Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul, that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
— 2 Samuel 9:1
Notice this carefully.
David was looking for Mephibosheth long before Mephibosheth was looking for David.
That alone will preach to somebody’s exhausted soul tonight.
Because many believers think they found God first.
No.
God was pursuing you while you were still hiding in fear.
Mephibosheth was living in a place called Lo-debar.

In Hebrew:
“לֹא דְבָר” (Lo Debar)

Literally:
“no pasture,”
“no word,”
“barren place,”
“place of nothingness.”
Trauma often pushes people into emotional Lo-debar.

You survive…
but you stop living.

You breathe…
but you stop expecting joy.

You exist…
but you stop believing anyone could genuinely love you.

You isolate.
You hide.
You shrink.
You assume your brokenness disqualifies you from belonging.
And then comes the moment that wrecks me every single time.
David summons Mephibosheth to the palace.
Imagine the terror.

Saul hunted David for years.
Ancient kings often exterminated surviving heirs to remove threats to the throne.
Mephibosheth probably believed this was his execution day.
Can you imagine his thoughts as they carried him into the palace?
“This is the end.”
Trauma always expects abandonment before mercy.
And when Mephibosheth arrives, Scripture says:

“And he fell on his face, and did reverence.”
— 2 Samuel 9:6
Then David says something that shattered decades of fear.

“Fear not.”
— 2 Samuel 9:7

In Hebrew:
“אַל־תִּירָא” (al-tira)
Do not fear.
The same words God repeatedly speaks throughout Scripture to traumatized people.

To Abraham.
To Isaac.
To Jacob.
To Hagar.
To Mary.
To Joseph.
To terrified disciples.
Because fear is humanity’s default language after pain.
But watch this carefully.
David does not merely spare Mephibosheth.
He restores him.

“And thou shalt eat bread at my table continually.”
— 2 Samuel 9:7
Continually.
Not temporarily.
Not conditionally.
Not until he “fixes himself.”
Continually.
This is one of the most breathtaking foreshadows of the Gospel in the Old Testament.
Because Mephibosheth arrives crippled…
but he eats like royalty.
He arrives broken…
but he is seated like family.
He arrives ashamed…
but covenant mercy speaks louder than his trauma.
And here is where the story becomes deeply personal for every believer reading this.
Many Christians are saved…
but still emotionally living in Lo-debar.

Still hiding.
Still ashamed.
Still expecting rejection.
Still defining themselves by where they fell.
But Jesus never asks wounded people to heal themselves before coming to His table.
Never.

The Gospel is not:
“Fix yourself so God can love you.”

The Gospel is:
Christ loved us while we were still broken.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”

The Greek word for commendeth is:
“συνίστησιν” (synistēsin)

meaning:
to demonstrate,
to prove,
to establish undeniably.
The cross was God proving His love toward spiritually crippled people.
Not polished people.
Not emotionally flawless people.
Broken people.
Somebody needs to hear this clearly:

Your trauma may explain your fears…
but it does not cancel your value.
Mephibosheth’s feet were crippled.
But his seat at the king’s table was secure.
And maybe that is why this story hits so hard for people carrying silent pain.
Because many of us know what it feels like to smile publicly while privately living crippled emotionally.
Some wounds do not bleed externally.
Some people have mastered looking “fine” while internally surviving panic, abandonment wounds, father wounds, church hurt, betrayal trauma, shame, grief, anxiety, and exhaustion.

But the Gospel still says:
there is room at the King’s table.
Not because you earned it.
Because Jesus made covenant mercy available through His blood.
Ephesians 2:13 says:
“But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.”

The Greek phrase:
“ἐγενήθητε ἐγγὺς” (egenēthēte engys)

means:
“brought near.”
That is the Gospel.
God brings near the people pain tried to exile.
And maybe the deepest part of Mephibosheth’s story is this:
He never stopped being crippled physically.
Scripture never says his legs were healed.
Yet he still belonged at the table.
Read that again slowly.
Because some believers secretly think God only loves the healed version of them.
No.
Christ’s love reaches people in process.

People with scars.
People with trauma.
People rebuilding after devastation.
People learning how to trust again.
People learning how to breathe again after years of emotional suffocation.
And if you are honest…
some of you are exhausted from pretending you are stronger than you actually are.
This story is for you.
The King still calls your name.
Not to shame you.
Not to expose you.
Not to destroy you.
But to bring you near.

To restore dignity.
To restore identity.
To restore belonging.
And the enemy desperately wants traumatized believers isolated because isolation distorts the voice of God.
That is why some of you need to stop hiding in Lo-debar emotionally.

Stop believing nobody could understand your pain.
Stop believing your damage ruined your purpose.
Stop believing God only uses emotionally unscarred people.
Mephibosheth’s story destroys that lie forever.
Because covenant mercy was stronger than inherited shame.
And maybe tonight, somebody reading this realizes for the first time:
“I have spent my whole life expecting rejection from a King who was actually preparing a seat for me.”
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
And somebody you love is secretly living in emotional Lo-debar right now pretending they are okay.
Because sometimes the people sitting quietly at the King’s table are the ones who survived the deepest falls.
